Here's what to know about what's formally known as daylight saving time as it ends for the year: What is daylight saving time, and why do we have it? Daylight saving time is the period during the year, from March to early November, when the majority of the U.S. operates one hour ahead of standard time. The move effectively "saves" an hour of daylight from the morning and adds it to the evening during the spring and summer months when the days are the longest. description: Lyn Dade and Lyn Collins respond to an article by John Humphrys about the 1966 disaster and the lessons that haven’t be learned John Humphrys’ righteous anger at the carelessness of national institutions and the horrors that followed as a result – at Aberfan, Hillsborough, Grenfell and during Covid – is matched only by his disgust at the lack of accountability afterwards ( At Aberfan, I saw fathers digging for their missing children. And the lessons society should have learned, it hasn’t, 24 October ). Sadly, it is too often true that those in leadership roles walk away with no more than a slapped wrist. In France, citizens would be manning the barricades. Here? “Dreadful, isn’t it?” Followed by a shrug. Like Humphrys, we should be raging at the death, grief and lasting trauma that were delivered by our “leaders”. But we don’t. Because we don’t believe that it will make any difference. description: The radical Stern report showed that a low-carbon future is also good economics. But it seems that capitalism needs a reminder Saving the only planet we have makes good economic sense. There is, after all, no money to be made on a dead Earth. There may be costs involved now, but they are worth paying to protect our children from certain destruction. These propositions seem self-evident now. But two decades ago, mainstream economists had very different ideas. They had proved that the climate crisis would be a mere economic blip, easily absorbed by growing economies and therefore not worth spending money on. In their accounting, they considered ice caps and glaciers functionally worthless, that trees only add to GDP when they are cut down, and that a livable climate shouldn’t even merit a line on a spreadsheet.
